# Leptospirosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Leptospirosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/kf0mm2)

---

## Summary

Leptospirosis is a <u>zoonotic disease</u> caused by gram-negative <u>Leptospira</u> bacteria. Direct transmission to humans occurs when broken <u>skin</u> and <u>mucous membranes</u> come into contact with the urine of infected animals, such as rodents. The early phase of the disease is mild and characterized by nonspecific symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>headache</u>, and <u>myalgia</u>). In most cases, symptoms resolve spontaneously after a week. However, in 10% of cases, the disease progresses rapidly to a severe form (<u>icterohemorrhagic leptospirosis</u>, or <u>Weil disease</u>), which typically manifests with a triad of <u>liver</u> failure, <u>acute kidney injury</u>, and <u>bleeding diathesis</u>. Diagnosis is based on <u>patient history</u>, clinical findings, and laboratory tests. Treatment consists of <u>antibiotics</u> and <u>supportive care</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Most commonly found in tropical climates [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)

* Worldwide <u>incidence</u> of ∼ 1 million cases resulting in ∼ 59,000 deaths annually [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)

* Most cases in the US and its territories occur in Hawaii or Puerto Rico or are associated with international travel. [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: Leptospira (especially <u>L. interrogans</u> sensu lato); , a genus of gram-negative <u>spirochete</u> with hook-shaped ends   [[2]](/library/gzWFHL0)

* Transmission [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)

* Sources

* Urine, blood, or tissue of an infected animal (most commonly rats)

* Environmental contamination (e.g., water contaminated with urine of infected animals)

* Entry points: broken <u>skin</u> or exposed <u>mucous membranes</u> (e.g., <u>conjunctiva</u>, oral <u>mucosa</u>)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Occupations that involve direct or indirect contact with animals (e.g., agricultural or sewage workers)

* Freshwater recreational activities (e.g., canoeing, swimming, windsurfing)

## Clinical features

Most infections are asymptomatic. Patients with symptoms generally present 1–2 weeks after exposure with a <u>self-limited</u> <u>flu-like illness</u>  that progresses to <u>multiple organ failure</u> in 5–10% of patients. [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)




### Mild leptospirosis (<u>anicteric leptospirosis</u>) [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)[[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)[[4]](/library/-DbDSD)




* Symptoms

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Headache</u>, <u>photophobia</u>

* <u>Myalgias</u>;  (especially the calves and lower back)

* <u>Vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>

* Signs

* Conjunctival suffusion: bilateral diffuse reddening of the <u>conjunctivae</u> without <u>exudates</u>

* Mild <u>jaundice</u>

* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* <u>Meningeal signs</u>

* <u>Rash</u>





![Eye signs in leptospirosis (conjunctival suffusion)](media/j6g7jrb20ix2ww67bqljnegp.jpg)

Eye signs in leptospirosis (conjunctival suffusion)




### Severe leptospirosis (<u>icteric leptospirosis</u>) [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)[[4]](/library/-DbDSD)




In addition to the signs and symptoms of <u>mild leptospirosis</u>, <u>severe leptospirosis</u> manifests with rapidly progressive <u>multiple organ failure</u> and may include the following:




* Classic triad of Weil disease

* <u>Signs of acute kidney injury</u> (e.g., <u>oliguria</u>, <u>anuria</u>)

* <u>Signs of liver failure</u> (e.g., <u>jaundice</u>)

* <u>Hemorrhagic diathesis</u> (e.g., <u>hemoptysis</u>, <u>purpura</u>, <u>melena</u>)

* <u>Clinical features of shock</u> (e.g., <u>hypotension</u>)

* Clinical features of cardiac inflammation: e.g., <u>myocarditis</u>, <u>pericarditis</u>, <u>arrhythmia</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Severe leptospirosis</u> has a high <u>mortality rate</u>. [[4]](/library/-DbDSD)

---

## Diagnosis

The initial diagnosis of leptospirosis requires a high index of suspicion because the clinical features are nonspecific. Do not delay treatment to obtain confirmatory studies.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)[[4]](/library/-DbDSD)[[5]](/library/IzWY8L0)




Laboratory findings are nonspecific but may help assess for <u>end-organ damage</u>.




* <u>CBC</u>: <u>leukocytosis</u> with <u>left shift</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>anemia</u>

* <u>Electrolytes</u>: <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>hypomagnesemia</u>

* <u>Renal function tests</u>: ↑ <u>creatinine</u>, ↑ <u>BUN</u>

* ↑ <u>ESR</u> and ↑ <u>CRP</u>

* <u>Liver function</u> tests: increased <u>bilirubin</u>, <u>AST</u>, <u>ALT</u>, and <u>ALP</u>

* ↑ <u>CPK</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>pyuria</u>, <u>microscopic hematuria</u>, <u>hyaline casts</u>, <u>granular casts</u>

* <u>CSF</u>: may show <u>pleocytosis</u>; protein and <u>glucose</u> levels are usually normal





### Confirmatory studies [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)[[4]](/library/-DbDSD)[[5]](/library/IzWY8L0)




A definitive diagnosis may be made based on direct detection or <u>serology</u>. [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)




* Direct detection from blood, urine, and/or <u>CSF</u> samples

* <u>PCR</u>

* <u>Dark-field microscopy</u>

* <u>Serology</u>

* Cannot be used for early diagnostic or treatment decisions  [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)

* Microscopic agglutination test (<u>MAT</u>): <u>gold standard</u> [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)[[5]](/library/IzWY8L0)

* Patient serum is incubated with <u>Leptospira</u> <u>serovars</u> and <u>titers</u> are obtained for positive reactions. [[6]](/library/rzWf8L0)

* Can only be performed at specific laboratories (e.g., <u>CDC</u> laboratories)





> [!NOTE]
> The thin <u>Leptospira</u> <u>spirochetes</u> cannot be visualized by <u>light microscopy</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Leptospirosis is a <u>notifiable disease</u> in the US; report confirmed cases to the <u>CDC</u>. [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)

## Treatment

### <u>Antibiotics</u> [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)[[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)




Start <u>antibiotics</u> immediately if leptospirosis is suspected; do not wait for <u>confirmatory testing</u>. [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)




* Options for <u>mild leptospirosis</u>

* <u>Doxycycline</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)

* <u>Amoxicillin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)

* <u>Ampicillin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)

* <u>Azithromycin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)

* Options for <u>severe leptospirosis</u>

* <u>Penicillin G</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)

* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)

* <u>Doxycycline</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Doxycycline</u> or <u>azithromycin</u> are preferred in regions where <u>rickettsial infections</u> are coendemic. [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)




> [!TIP]
> Initiation of <u>antibiotic therapy</u> may cause a <u>Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction</u>. [[1]](/library/SzWyHL0)




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[3]](/library/ObWIFP0)




* Renal dysfunction

* <u>IV fluid therapy</u>

* <u>Electrolyte repletion</u>

* Dialysis in patients with <u>oliguric</u> <u>renal failure</u>

* <u>Respiratory failure</u>: <u>mechanical ventilation</u> using <u>lung protective ventilation</u> strategies





### Disposition [[4]](/library/-DbDSD)[[7]](/library/BzWzEL0)




* <u>Severe leptospirosis</u>: Admit to the <u>ICU</u>.

* Moderate leptospirosis: Admit to a monitored bed.

* <u>Mild leptospirosis</u>: Discharge with close follow-up and strict <u>return precautions</u> if symptoms of <u>end-organ damage</u> occur (e.g., <u>oliguria</u>, <u>jaundice</u>).
